title: "Automate a Python Data Pipeline with GitHub Actions"

## Introduction: let a script do its job on a schedule

Suppose you want a new row of data every day. You could remember to run a script each morning, but sooner or later you'll forget. You could leave your laptop on, but then the job stops when the laptop sleeps. **GitHub Actions** gives your repository a small, temporary computer that can run the script for you.

In this tutorial, we'll build the idea step by step: tell GitHub *when* to start, show it *what* to run, and save the result before its computer goes away. Our example is [Archidekt Snapshot](https://github.com/jimna-h/archidekt-snapshot), which tracks decks in a public Archidekt folder. You don't need to know anything about Magic: The Gathering; the same pattern works for many Python scripts that produce data files.

## 1. Two parts: the script and the instructions

Think of the Python script as the worker and the Actions workflow as its instruction sheet. The worker, [`track_prices.py`](https://github.com/jimna-h/archidekt-snapshot/blob/main/track_prices.py), fetches deck and price data from Archidekt and writes CSV files under `data/`. The workflow, [`.github/workflows/daily-prices.yml`](https://github.com/jimna-h/archidekt-snapshot/blob/main/.github/workflows/daily-prices.yml), tells GitHub when to start that worker and what to do with its files.

The script needs to know which Archidekt folder to read. It gets the folder number from an **environment variable**: a setting supplied when the script starts. In this workflow, the setting is named `ARCHIDEKT_FOLDER_ID`.

The script writes daily totals to `data/totals.csv`. If it runs twice in one day, the second run replaces that day's rows instead of adding duplicates.

## 2. Tell GitHub when and what to run

An Actions workflow is a YAML file: a list of instructions with indentation showing which instructions belong together. Each run starts on a **runner**, GitHub's temporary computer. The example's main steps are:

```yaml
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 13 * * *"
    - cron: "47 16 * * *"
    - cron: "23 21 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: [track_prices.py, .github/workflows/daily-prices.yml]

jobs:
  snapshot:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v6
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: python track_prices.py
        env:
          ARCHIDEKT_FOLDER_ID: ${{ vars.ARCHIDEKT_FOLDER_ID }}
```

Read the top as the *when* and the bottom as the *what*:

- `schedule` starts the job at set times. The `cron` text describes those times.
- `workflow_dispatch` adds a button so you can start a run yourself.
- `push` starts a new snapshot when the script or workflow changes on `main`.
- `checkout` puts a copy of your repository on the runner. The next steps install Python 3.12 and the packages listed in `requirements.txt`.
- `run` starts the script. The `env` setting gives it the folder number it needs. Add `ARCHIDEKT_FOLDER_ID` in **Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions > Variables**.

### What does the schedule mean?

The cron expression has five fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month, and day of the week. In `17 13 * * *`, the first two values mean “minute 17 of hour 13”; the stars mean “every day, every month, every weekday.” This workflow uses UTC, which stays fixed when Mountain Time changes for daylight saving.

| Cron | UTC | Mountain in summer | Mountain in winter | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `17 13 * * *` | 13:17 | 7:17 a.m. | 6:17 a.m. | Main run |
| `47 16 * * *` | 16:47 | 10:47 a.m. | 9:47 a.m. | Backup |
| `23 21 * * *` | 21:23 | 3:23 p.m. | 2:23 p.m. | Backup |

Why three times? GitHub can delay a scheduled run when Actions is busy or occasionally miss one. Each backup checks whether today's snapshot is already in `totals.csv`; it exits if so, and collects data if not. A schedule means “try around this time,” not “run exactly on time.” GitHub also supports a time zone setting for local-time schedules. See [GitHub's schedule documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

## 3. Keep the result after the runner goes away

The runner is temporary: when the job finishes, GitHub throws that computer away. The files the script created would disappear too unless the workflow saves them back to the repository. To let the workflow push a commit, give its built-in token permission to write repository contents:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: write
```

Then the workflow stages the new files and commits them when they changed. These are the key Git commands from the example:

```bash
git add data/
git diff --cached --quiet || git commit -m "Snapshot today's data"
git push
```

`git add` selects the files to save. `git diff --cached --quiet` checks whether any selected files changed. If they did, `||` runs the commit command; if nothing changed, there is no empty commit to make. Finally, `git push` sends the commit back to GitHub. The repository's Actions settings must also allow a read-and-write token.

The production workflow also retries if someone edits the repository during a run, and uses `actions: write` to keep its schedule enabled. See the [complete workflow](https://github.com/jimna-h/archidekt-snapshot/blob/main/.github/workflows/daily-prices.yml) for these safeguards.

Committing files is one way to save results. You can also send them to an external database, such as PostgreSQL, if it is reachable from the runner. Keep database credentials in [GitHub Actions Secrets](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets), not in the workflow file. This project uses CSVs because they're easy to inspect and version.

## 4. Start a run and see if it worked

Before trusting the schedule, try a manual run. Push the workflow to `main`, open **Actions > Daily snapshot > Run workflow**, and click the button. Check each step's log for errors. A successful run should finish with a new “Snapshot” commit when the data changed.

You can also look at the result. After a week of snapshots, `totals.csv` can show whether one deck's estimated value has moved. This chart reads the project's public CSV files from GitHub when the Quarto page is rendered:

```{python}
#| label: fig-deck-value
#| fig-cap: "One deck's TCGplayer value across daily snapshots."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart showing the TCGplayer value of one deck over time."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

repo = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jimna-h/archidekt-snapshot/main/data"
totals = pd.read_csv(f"{repo}/totals.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
decks = pd.read_csv(f"{repo}/decks.csv", usecols=["deck_id", "deck_name"])

deck = totals.merge(decks, on="deck_id")
deck = deck[deck["deck_name"].str.startswith("3. Hungry Like the Sleuth")]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.plot(deck["date"], deck["tcg_total"], marker="o")
ax.set(ylabel="Deck value (USD)", title=deck["deck_name"].iloc[0])
fig.autofmt_xdate()
plt.show()
```

If the workflow can't push, check both `contents: write` and the repository's Actions permissions. If a public repository is inactive for 60 days, GitHub may disable its schedule.

## Conclusion: try the pattern on your own data

The process is **choose a trigger, prepare the runner, run your script, save the output, and check the result**. The script can change while the Actions steps stay similar.

For practice, pick one number you'd like to track, such as a daily temperature. First add a manual trigger and confirm that the workflow saves a result. Then add a schedule. After a few runs, you'll have a small dataset you collected automatically. The [Archidekt Snapshot repository](https://github.com/jimna-h/archidekt-snapshot) is available if you'd like to compare your workflow with the full example.
